source: Keane, Brayshaw (1988) The Incremental Analogy Machine (IAM)
finding: IAM maps a small subset of the base serially, under a working-memory-like limit, instead of building all matches at once as SME does. Not read in full this session; known only via the series plan.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Original paper not opened. Wikipedia route unverified. Treat as background.
agent_relevance: Serial, small-chunk mapping is a design pattern: map a few relations, then extend.

source: Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994) Constraints on analogical mapping: a comparison of three models
finding: Compares SME, ACME and IAM against human data on how mapping order and constraint pressure affect mapping. IAM predicts order effects of serial mapping.
numbers: Not read; no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened. Cited from memory of the field.
agent_relevance: Order of presentation can change a mapping; a serial mapper should vary order and compare.

source: Hummel, Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: LISA
finding: LISA maps by serial activation of one proposition at a time, with a working-memory-like limit that falls out of binding by time.
numbers: Not read; no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A model for chunked mapping with an explicit capacity bound.

source: Halford, Wilson, Phillips (1998) Processing capacity defined by relational complexity
finding: Cited by Webb et al. (2023) as the source of the claim that analogy difficulty tracks relational complexity, the number of unique relations processed in parallel.
numbers: Not read; only the citation was seen in the Webb 2023 reference list.
limits: Citation seen, source not opened.
agent_relevance: A measurable difficulty dial: count relations that must be bound at once.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on novel Digit Matrix problems with no prompt and no examples. The pattern of errors by problem type resembled humans.
numbers: Digit Matrices, humans N=40. Generative: odds ratio GPT-3 vs humans 1.88 (p=0.005, CI 1.21-2.91). Multiple choice: OR 6.27 (p=2.3e-8, CI 3.28-11.99). Item-level correlation GPT-3 vs humans r(30)=0.39, p=0.027.
limits: Best human scored 100%. Hodel and West and Lewis and Mitchell later showed fragility.
agent_relevance: Evidence LLMs can map without an explicit capacity-bounded mapper. Do not assume robustness.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Difficulty rose with number of distinct rules in a problem, even when total rules were held constant. This is the signature predicted by working-memory-limited mapping, and GPT-3 showed it too.
numbers: GPT-3 progression vs no-progression rules: OR 0.07 (p=1.9e-5, CI 0.02-0.24). Humans: OR 0.41 (p=0.0001, CI 0.24-0.69). Problem type (one, two, three rules, logic) effect on generative accuracy OR 0.5 (p=2e-16).
limits: Correlation with load is not proof of a capacity limit in the model.
agent_relevance: Count of unique relations is a usable complexity measure. Split multi-rule problems into one-rule steps.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: On verbal and story analogies GPT-3 equalled or beat people.
numbers: Datasets: UCLA VAT (human N=57), Sternberg and Nigro (N=20), SAT analogies (5 choices, chance 20%), Jones et al. (N=241), story analogies (N=54).
limits: Mostly familiar problem types, so training contamination is possible.
agent_relevance: Strong zero-shot analogy is plausible for frontier models on familiar types.

source: Hodel, West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Changing letter-string problems slightly (synthetic alphabet) collapses GPT-3 while humans stay level. Argues the original claim of general analogy is not supported.
numbers: Synthetic-alphabet tasks extend, successor, predecessor, fix alphabet: GPT-3 generative accuracy below 0.1. Only remove-redundant and sort stay near original. Average over N=50 instances.
limits: Only GPT-3 tested. Counterfactual comprehension checks show GPT-3 understood the new alphabet (at least 30% of original level on all but one check).
agent_relevance: Failure on permuted alphabet is a failure to hold a long index chain, not to see the relation. Give the agent a tool or written index table.

source: Lewis, Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 drop sharply on counterfactual letter-string analogies; humans do not. The gap persists for GPT-4.
numbers: Human N=46 (their sample) vs N=57 (Webb). Best prompt was Hodel and West style with the alphabet listed. Counterfactual comprehension checks mostly high, so models grasp the rule.
limits: Prompt choice mattered. Authors do not test code tools.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting is brittle; test any agent loop on permuted or counterfactual variants.

source: Webb, Mondal, Cohen (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Counterfactual failure was due to counting letters by position. GPT-4 with code execution solved the permuted-alphabet problems at human level.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). GPT-4 vs humans P=8.9e-13 (humans better). GPT-4 plus code vs humans P=0.496 (no difference). Errors based on a valid alternative rule: GPT-4 46%, humans 39%.
limits: Code use is not human-like. Authors note capacity-limited numerosity in humans as a parallel.
agent_relevance: Offloading a bounded sub-step (indexing) to a tool restores mapping. Fits a tool-assisted scaffold.
quote: GPT-4 was able to solve these 'counterfactual' letter-string analogies at a roughly human level of performance when given the ability to count using code execution

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) shows a human-like n-back pattern: sensitivity d' falls to about 1 at n=3. Capacity is about 3 in three of four verbal variants.
numbers: Verbal n=1,2,3. Variants: base, noise, feedback, CoT. Noise cut capacity.
limits: Single model in depth; GPT-4 only to n=3. A larger spatial grid gave higher capacity, unexplained.
agent_relevance: A measured working-memory-like ceiling (about 3 items) to set chunk size in a serial mapper.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: Other LLMs have very low capacity. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are better, GPT-4 far above others.
numbers: Seven other models tested (Bloomz-7B, 7B1-mt, ChatGLM-6B v1.0 and v1.1, Vicuna-7B, Vicuna-13B): nearly indistinguishable, very low capacity. GPT-4 not tested beyond n=3.
limits: Cost limited testing.
agent_relevance: Capacity grows with model; schema chunk size should depend on model.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: Distractor symbols lower capacity, like human distractor studies.
numbers: Noise variant: 3-6 random symbols per trial; d' is lower than other variants.
limits: Noise design is an author construct.
agent_relevance: Keep irrelevant detail out of the mapping context. Prune before mapping.

source: Huang et al. (2025) On the failure of latent state persistence in LLMs (v1 titled: Language models do not have human-like working memory)
finding: LLMs do not hold a hidden internal state across turns. They fail to allocate probability to one hidden choice, drift across yes-no questions, and fail to track transformations of hidden variables.
numbers: Three experiments: Number Guessing Game, Yes-No Game, hidden-variable tracking. Exact rates not read.
limits: Tests hidden-state persistence, not mapping directly.
agent_relevance: Mapping state must be written into context. Do not rely on the model remembering a partial mapping silently.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) United minds or isolated agents? Coordination of LLMs under cognitive load theory (CoThinker)
finding: A multi-agent setup built on cognitive load theory helps most when intrinsic load is high. On low-load instruction tasks, coordination overhead hurts.
numbers: Gains reported: reasoning +15.5% vs CoT (p=0.001); data analysis +16.2% vs IO (p<.001); language +18.3% vs SR (p<.001); another row +31.2% vs CoT (p=0.006); one row +123.6% vs MAD (p<.001).
limits: Row labels were partly truncated in extraction; read the tables for exact tasks. The working-memory link is a design lens, not proof.
agent_relevance: Splitting a big mapping across specialist agents or steps pays only when the task is heavy; skip for easy cases.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Telling the model to recall related problems before solving, in one prompt, beat 0-shot and few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K: 5-shot CoT 75.0% vs self-generated exemplars about 76-78% (GPT-3.5-turbo); text-davinci-003 14.8% to 50.3-61.0%; PaLM2 60.8% to 78.2-81.7%. MATH GPT-3.5-turbo 33.0% to 33.9-37.3%. Authors report average +4%.
limits: Row order in the extracted table is ambiguous; sizes are right but the variant assignment is approximate.
agent_relevance: A cheap analog-retrieval step; not capacity-limited mapping itself.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Language encodings of Raven items let LMs solve them zero-shot; the level of abstraction in the encoding mattered a lot.
numbers: Reported accuracies range from about 14% to 95.6% by configuration and model; 2x2Grid 54.0% to 81.8%, 3x3Grid 73.0% to 86.4% across encodings; OPT 1.3B 47.2% to 72.0%.
limits: Values read from a table whose column labels were lost in extraction.
agent_relevance: How the problem is chunked and encoded moves accuracy by tens of points.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus and Llama-405B match humans on semantic structure-mapping in several conditions but react differently to semantic distractors.
numbers: Metric is match-to-reference. GPT-4 about 0.9, Llama-405B about 0.5 in the Only RHS condition. Claude 3 drops by 0.5 in one distractor condition. Chance baseline for RHS-only 25%.
limits: Match-to-reference is not plain accuracy.
agent_relevance: Distractor sensitivity is a mapping risk; keep distractors out.

source: Mondal, Cohen, Webb (2024) Slot Abstractors: toward scalable abstract visual reasoning
finding: A relational-bottleneck model with object slots beats earlier models on abstract visual reasoning.
numbers: V-PROM 67.7% vs 51.2% for Relation Net (previous best). Ablated variant 30.01%. Gains up to 9% on tasks, 3% average over prior state of the art.
limits: Visual domain, trained model, not a prompt method.
agent_relevance: A bounded relational bottleneck helps generalisation; weak transfer to a prompt scaffold.

source: Webb, Sinha, Cohen (2021) Emergent symbols through binding in external memory (ESBN)
finding: A network with a separate external memory binding variables to values generalises relational rules out of distribution.
numbers: Nearly perfect generalisation (95% or higher) of the learned rule on all four tasks.
limits: Small trained model on synthetic tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit external store for the current partial mapping.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024), Codeforces and BIG-Bench
finding: Self-generated knowledge plus exemplars gave further gains on hard code tasks.
numbers: Codeforces Acc@1 GPT-4: 16% (0-shot CoT) to 19% with knowledge plus exemplars; Acc@10 30% to 37%. GPT-3.5-turbo-16k 8% to 15% Acc@1 (assignment of rows approximate).
limits: Table layout garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Recall-then-solve is a cheap add-on step.
